### In Praise of the Unfinished

Every neighborhood has a window with a project in it: a chair stripped to its pale wood, a model ship waiting for rigging, a pile of fabric held together by pins and optimism. From the street, these things can look like evidence of failure. Up close, they are more interesting. They are objects with their future still showing.

I am suspicious of the satisfaction I get from crossing things off lists. The line through the word is so clean. It offers the small, illicit pleasure of a door closing. But most worthwhile work happens before the door closes, when the room is still drafty and anyone might walk in with a better idea.

A recipe becomes itself in the corrections: *less salt*, *Nina uses plums*, *don’t bake at Mum’s*. A half-learned song is all possibility and wrong notes; your hands keep proposing routes your ears reject. Even a conversation has its best moments just before either person knows quite what they mean. You say, “No, not exactly,” and try again. For a few seconds, you are not performing a self. You are making one.

This is not an argument for leaving everything half done. The world needs roofs that keep out rain and messages that actually get sent. Some unfinished things are not open; they are avoided. There is a difference between a pause and a hiding place, and usually you can tell by whether returning gives you energy or requires an excuse.

Still, I hope there is always one thing in a life that resists completion: a language whose grammar remains slightly outrageous, a garden with an unreasonable corner, a notebook containing more questions than conclusions. Something that cannot be crossed off because it keeps changing the list.

An unfinished thing asks for a particular kind of loyalty. Not the loyalty of staring at it every day, but of coming back. Sanding one arm of the chair. Looking up one word. Playing the four difficult bars slowly enough to hear what they have been trying to say.

Perhaps a good day is not one in which everything is finished. Perhaps it is one in which something has been moved, however slightly, from *someday* to *again*.
